learningObjective: Trace how a versioned policy becomes per-policy decisions while human review and appeals correct decisions and supply evidence for evaluation and retraining.
mediumRationale: A compact top-to-bottom Mermaid flow is the smallest medium that keeps policy ownership separate from model scoring while showing the allow, review, and auto-action routes and their shared correction loop.

mediumComparison.mermaid: Selected: labelled directed edges make responsibility, routing, and feedback explicit, while the established renderer supplies responsive layout and theme support.
mediumComparison.svg: Rejected: the lesson is an architecture and lifecycle rather than quantitative geometry, so fixed coordinates would add maintenance without improving the causal sequence.
mediumComparison.semanticHtml: Rejected: cards or a table could compare actions but would weaken the converging policy-and-score inputs and the review and appeal feedback paths.
mediumComparison.interaction: Rejected: changing thresholds interactively would teach calibration tradeoffs, but the article's harder mental model is policy governance plus operational feedback, which is fixed and should remain available without JavaScript.
mediumComparison.paperReuse: Rejected: the reviewed sources contain related moderation taxonomies and process guidance, but no single figure expresses this article's architecture. Figure reuse permission was not established, and no source composition is copied.
mediumComparison.noVisual: Rejected: the prose names layers and senior-level additions in separate sections, leaving readers to assemble where policy ends, model scoring begins, and corrected decisions return to the system.

pages.insight: The preceding algorithms pros-and-cons divider closes the prior topic and contains no content-moderation, policy, review, or appeals architecture.
The classification loss and evaluation divider begins the nearest relevant neighborhood but provides no moderation workflow.
The classification-metrics slide defines precision, recall, and the ROC operating-point tradeoff, supporting per-policy evaluation rather than a single accuracy number.
The neighboring evaluation slide shows how moving a classifier threshold trades recall against false positives, but it does not connect thresholds to policy-specific actions or human review.
The calibration and out-of-distribution slide links meaningful confidence to threshold-based rejection, the closest deck analogue to routing borderline cases for review.
The general-neural-networks divider ends the relevant classification neighborhood and confirms that no adjacent moderation-system treatment follows.

deckReview.notes: The complete 214-page local deck was text-indexed for moderation, content policy, human review, appeals, enforcement, and closely related classifier, threshold, precision, recall, and calibration terms. It contains no content-moderation system or appeals workflow. Pages 31-40 were inspected as the nearest classification operating-policy neighborhood; pages 37-39 provide useful metric, threshold, and calibration context only. No deck artwork, wording, coordinates, or layout is reused.

sources.title: Algorithmic content moderation: Technical and political challenges in the automation of platform governance
sources.usage: Used as the primary research source for the sequence from matching or prediction through a decision to a governance outcome, and for the limits of automated context-dependent decisions.
sources.license: The article is publicly readable, but figure-reuse permission was not relied on or assumed. No figure, example, data, wording, or layout is copied; the shipped flow is independently authored.

sources.title: The Santa Clara Principles on Transparency and Accountability in Content Moderation
sources.usage: Used as authoritative civil-society guidance to verify that clear rules, notice, human support, appeals, cultural competence, and reporting on successful and unsuccessful appeals are parts of accountable moderation.
sources.license: No explicit license granting reuse of site text or artwork was identified. The principles are cited for process requirements only; no prose, graphic, icon, or layout is adapted.

sources.title: NIST AI Risk Management Framework 1.0
sources.usage: Used as official risk-management guidance to cross-check the separation of governance, measurement, and management responsibilities across an AI system lifecycle.
sources.license: NIST publications are generally not subject to U.S. copyright, but no NIST figure is needed or reused. The visual is an original application-specific synthesis.

sourceReview.notes: The hardest prose-only mental model is not the classifier itself but the governed decision loop: one item receives separate policy scores; a versioned policy determines per-policy thresholds and actions; uncertain cases go to trained reviewers; auto-actions need notice and appeal; and corrected decisions become evaluation and training evidence rather than silently redefining policy. Source figures were unnecessary, and unclear artwork permissions triggered the default original-redraw treatment.

agentReview.summary: Read the complete article, text-indexed all 214 deck pages and inspected the neighboring classification slides, then reviewed a primary algorithmic-moderation paper, the Santa Clara Principles, and the official NIST AI RMF before selecting an original compact Mermaid decision-and-correction flow.

implementation.accessibility: The Mermaid block provides a specific accessible title and a complete description. Every responsibility, action, and feedback path is directly labelled, and node text plus solid and dashed edge semantics preserve the lesson without color. The top-to-bottom compact layout is designed for the reading column at 390 CSS pixels; the shared Mermaid theme handles dark mode and print.
